title: The Long Way Home: 3 September 1951
dramaticQuestion: When damage removes the safe option, can disciplined observation and aircraft handling preserve enough control to choose survival over the machine?

perspective.actorRole: Ensign Neil A. Armstrong flying a VF-51 Panther from USS Essex

sorties.playerFantasy: Fly the documented cable-strike sequence as a young naval aviator whose survival depends on precise handling and a wingman's external inspection.
sorties.scenarioSummary: On 3 September 1951 Armstrong launches from USS Essex in an F9F-2, joins Major John Carpenter for armed reconnaissance west of Wonsan, strikes what he later recalled as a cable at low altitude, stabilizes the Panther after losing part of the right wing, and flies south before ejecting in friendly territory.
sorties.centralDecision: Use aircraft response and Carpenter's bounded visual report to preserve control, reject an unsafe landing, and reach a defensible ejection area.
sorties.failureMeaning: A restart identifies the first controllable route, collision, stabilization, formation, or ejection error without allowing the fixed historical sequence to branch into an alternate biography.
sorties.successMeaning: The player performs the documented survival sequence competently while the debrief separates recorded history from authored route, damage, dialogue, and system reconstruction.

perspective.actorRole: Fictional coalition pilot managing battle damage and uncertain recovery options

sorties.playerFantasy: Reapply the historical discipline under modern pressure: stabilize first, ask a wingman for observable facts, and choose a recovery plan without hidden simulation truth.
sorties.scenarioSummary: A fictional 2034 aircraft takes control-surface damage while the network is degraded. The player must separate cockpit evidence from a wingman's limited inspection, then choose a divert, controlled ejection, or continued flight within an authored safety envelope.
sorties.centralDecision: Decide which recovery option the available evidence actually supports instead of treating advanced displays or a wingman's estimate as certainty.
sorties.failureMeaning: The debrief distinguishes an evidence error from a handling error and preserves an alternate launchable route rather than turning one mistake into a hidden run-ending penalty.
sorties.successMeaning: The player carries Armstrong's stabilization-and-inspection lesson into a different fictional aircraft and makes a defensible survival decision from observer-safe evidence.

echoes.constant: A damaged aircraft supplies incomplete evidence through control response, instruments, visible structure, and another pilot's observation.
echoes.changed: The historical Panther has sparse instruments and direct formation inspection; the fictional modern aircraft has denser but still fallible status and network information.
echoes.dramaticPurpose: Make Armstrong's survival problem change how the player interprets modern aircraft status, rather than using the historical sortie as detached biography.

echoes.constant: Competent airmanship includes recognizing when preserving the aircraft is no longer the safest achievable outcome.
echoes.changed: Armstrong's broad outcome is fixed by history; the fictional modern sortie allows several evidence-bounded recovery outcomes without rewriting a real person's life.
echoes.dramaticPurpose: Turn ejection from spectacle into a reasoned survival decision whose logic can transfer to later play.

archiveEntries.title: Cable, Wing Loss, and the Limits of Reconstruction

claims.label: history
claims.statement: On 3 September 1951, contemporary records identify Ensign Neil A. Armstrong's VF-51 loss as an F9F-2, record BuNo 125122, and place his bailout near K-3 during USS Essex's Korean War deployment.
claims.qualification: The contemporary USS Essex report dates the loss to 3 September and identifies BuNo 125122 and Armstrong; the contemporary CVG-5 report identifies VF-51's type as F9F-2 and records the same date and damage sequence. The DPAA register and NHHC photograph catalog independently corroborate 3 September, and DPAA also records F9F-2. H-Gram 033's later 5 September/F9F-3 description is retained as a disclosed synthesis error, not treated as equal evidence. A separate NHHC bureau-number appendix assigns the 125080-125152 block, which includes 125122, to F9F-5. The incident-specific records control the mission-level F9F-2 identity, but that catalog anomaly keeps the individual airframe's delivered configuration, suffix, cockpit, engine, markings, loadout, and damaged aerodynamics open pending its aircraft history card. Use USS Essex (CV-9), not its later CVA designation, in 1951 presentation.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: The incident occurred during armed reconnaissance against transportation or storage targets west of Wonsan, associated by archival metadata with the Majon-ni area.
claims.qualification: The page-reviewed Essex and CVG-5 reports establish the date, aircraft loss, very hilly terrain, and a heavily loaded aircraft, but do not close the exact target, coordinates, corridor, formation size, attack direction, loadout, or the distinction between the flight's planned targets and Armstrong's own pass. Those details remain reconstruction until mission-plan, map, and ordnance records close them.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: Armstrong later recalled that his Panther struck a cable during the low-level mission and denied that antiaircraft fire directly caused the damage.
claims.qualification: This is Armstrong's retrospective account recorded roughly fifty years later. The page-reviewed contemporary Essex report attributes locked controls to enemy antiaircraft fire; the CVG-5 report attributes lost elevator control to antiaircraft fire and two feet of starboard-wing loss to a power pole. Preserve that conflict visibly. The mission may reconstruct one cable from Armstrong's account without claiming a historically mapped cable field or silently replacing the contemporary account.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: Armstrong recalled that the cable removed approximately six to eight feet from the Panther's right wing and left the aircraft flyable at speed.
claims.qualification: Six to eight feet is Armstrong's retrospective estimate; the contemporary CVG-5 report says two feet were sheared from the starboard wing on a power pole. Neither is a measured fracture record. The exact break geometry, aileron and tip-tank state, fuel and mass effects, and aerodynamic derivatives remain unresolved, and the seven-foot gameplay profile remains explicitly an oral-history reconstruction.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: Armstrong identified USAF Major John Carpenter, an exchange officer, as his flight lead and recalled Carpenter flying alongside the damaged aircraft.
claims.qualification: The current source does not establish the exact formation geometry, inspection duration, observations, or radio wording. Carpenter's runtime report must remain observer-safe and procedurally reconstructed.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: Armstrong recalled that he and Carpenter judged slowing the damaged Panther for landing could produce an uncontrollable snap and therefore chose ejection.
claims.qualification: Armstrong's account supports the joint reasoning in broad form. The contemporary CVG-5 report independently records lost elevator control and a required landing speed above 170 knots before ejection, but does not close exact dialogue, a tested safe-speed envelope, which landing alternatives were discussed, or the precise division of judgment between the two pilots.

claims.label: history
claims.statement: Armstrong recalled flying south into friendly territory, ejecting near Pohang or K-3, and being met by Marine lieutenant Goodell Warren in a jeep.
claims.qualification: The Essex report records bailout over friendly K-3; the CVG-5 report records seat clearance, manual chute opening, and landing near K-3. Armstrong's later account adds the southbound plan, ejection near Pohang/K-3, and recovery by Goodell Warren. The later H-Gram synthesis, not Armstrong's interview, adds that wind carried the parachute back over land. Exact ejection coordinates, intended disposal corridor, wind, parachute path, landing surface, recovery route, vehicle appearance, interaction, and words remain uncorroborated. Ground-recovery staging cannot be presented as exact history.

claims.label: reconstruction
claims.statement: Armstrong later described an old-style shotgun-shell-powered ejection seat and a 22-G seat load, but the current intake does not establish the exact Panther seat model, operating sequence, envelope, or acceleration history to be simulated.
claims.qualification: The cartridge description and 22-G figure are source-registered as Armstrong's first-person recollection, not as engineering source lock or a simulation parameter. Ejection and parachute implementation remains blocked on a provenance-verified 1951 Panther handbook, maintenance material, and appropriate technical review.

claims.label: reconstruction
claims.statement: Any playable sequence of multiple cable obstacles, their supports, spacing, height, purpose, and placement along an authored attack route is a gameplay reconstruction around the documented cable contact.
claims.qualification: The current sources establish a reported cable strike, not the exact local obstacle layout or even that multiple cables formed a deliberate antiaircraft field. Physical gameplay geometry must be tactically plausible, visibly disclosed as reconstruction, and must not masquerade as a map of the historical installation.

claims.label: reconstruction
claims.statement: A survivable partial-right-wing damage model can reproduce the reported scale and qualitative control problem only as a bounded public-data reconstruction, not as the exact aerodynamics of Armstrong's aircraft.
claims.qualification: Release requires sourced Panther geometry and controls, damage analogs, a sensitivity study, and declared playable bounds. Current sources support reported wing loss and landing risk but not fracture mechanics, damaged derivatives, fuel effects, or one exact recovery envelope.

claims.label: fiction
claims.statement: The 2034 damaged-aircraft diversion, its pilot, damage event, wingman, network state, recovery options, and outcomes are campaign fiction created to reapply the historical learning objective.
claims.qualification: The sortie may reuse declared public engineering constraints, but it is not presented as a prediction, real incident, or evidence about a future Korean conflict.

sources.title: The Spoken Word II: Recollections of Dryden History, Beyond the Sky
sources.perspective: Armstrong's first-person retrospective account on pages 16-18, recorded approximately fifty years after the event. It supports what Armstrong remembered, including his old-style shotgun-shell-powered and 22-G ejection-seat description, and the historical anchors used by the reconstruction; it is not a contemporary mission record, radio transcript, seat manual, cable survey, engineering acceleration trace, or damaged-aerodynamics dataset.

sources.title: H-Gram 033
sources.perspective: Later official U.S. Navy synthesis, especially pages 25-26, that identifies VF-51, USS Essex, the broad mission and competing incident accounts and says wind carried Armstrong's parachute back over land. Its 5 September/F9F-3 description is contradicted by the page-reviewed contemporary Essex and CVG-5 reports, and the exact drift path is uncorroborated; it remains useful for synthesis and source discovery, not as controlling evidence for date, subtype, or playable trajectory.

sources.title: Ensign Neil Armstrong, F9F Pilot, Korean War Recon Mission, Wonsan
sources.perspective: Official archival catalog metadata linking the image to a 3 September 1951 reconnaissance mission against transportation and storage facilities south of Majon-ni, west of Wonsan. Its 'shot down' caption does not resolve the damage mechanism or complete sortie sequence.

sources.title: Korean War Air Loss Database by Name
sources.perspective: Official Department of Defense loss-register entry on PDF page 4 records Neil A. Armstrong, USN, date 3 September 1951, VF-51, F9F-2, BuNo 125122, and USS Essex. It is strong structured corroboration for identity, date, unit, subtype, bureau number, and carrier, but it is a compiled database rather than the incident report and does not establish the target, damage mechanism, radio, ejection sequence, or recovery details.

sources.title: United States Naval Aviation 1910-1995, Appendix 9: Naval Aircraft Bureau Numbers
sources.publisher: Naval Historical Center, via Naval History and Heritage Command
sources.perspective: Official compiled bureau-number appendix, PDF page 38 and printed page 554, assigns the 125080-125152 block to F9F-5, creating a catalog anomaly for the Essex report's BuNo 125122 and the incident-specific F9F-2 identification. It does not override the contemporary air-group type table or identify the individual aircraft's delivered state; the aircraft history card is required before configuration, suffix, engine, cockpit batch, or markings are locked.

sources.title: Action Report for the Period, 18 August 1951 to 21 September 1951
sources.publisher: Commanding Officer, USS Essex (CV-9), via Naval History and Heritage Command
sources.perspective: Contemporary USS Essex Serial 093, page-reviewed at scan and printed page 3. Its 3 September chronology identifies F9F BuNo 125122 and Ensign Armstrong, attributes locked controls to enemy antiaircraft fire, records that control was regained, and records bailout over friendly K-3 before the aircraft burned. The cited URI is an intact Internet Archive capture of the original NHHC PDF asset because the live legacy asset path currently returns 404; NHHC's Essex action-report catalog remains the provenance landing page.

sources.title: Action Report of Carrier Air Group Five, 18 August 1951 to 19 September 1951
sources.publisher: Commander, Carrier Air Group Five, via Naval History and Heritage Command
sources.perspective: Contemporary CVG5/A16-13 Serial 065-51. Page 1 identifies VF-51's aircraft type as F9F-2; pages 4-5 place Armstrong's event on 3 September and record the report's antiaircraft-fire and power-pole account, lost elevator control, heavy ordnance, two feet of starboard-wing loss, a landing speed above 170 knots, ejection, seat clearance, manual chute opening, and landing near K-3. Page 12 carries the VF-51 F9F-2 type through the 3 September damage entries. The cited URI is an intact Internet Archive capture of the original NHHC asset; NHHC's carrier-air-group action-report catalog remains the provenance landing page.

sources.title: Armstrong cable-strike source register, intake snapshot
sources.perspective: Internal intake record used only to prove the declared research gaps and reconstruction boundaries. It is not historical evidence for the incident, not a technical source, not source lock, and not permission to ship any research asset it indexes.

abstractions.description: Titles and briefings use 3 September 1951 and the incident-level F9F-2 identity because the page-reviewed contemporary reports close the date and identify VF-51's aircraft type; later synthesis disagreements and the BuNo catalog anomaly remain disclosed in the archive.
abstractions.reason: The USS Essex chronology identifies Armstrong and BuNo 125122 on 3 September, while the CVG-5 report identifies VF-51 as F9F-2 and records the same date and event. Those incident-specific records outweigh H-Gram 033's later 5 September/F9F-3 description for mission identity, but NHHC's generic assignment of the 125122 block to F9F-5 prevents exact individual-airframe configuration lock before its history card is reviewed.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: The historical note explains the primary-record basis for 3 September and the mission's F9F-2 treatment, preserves the later synthesis disagreement, and discloses that the BuNo appendix conflict leaves the individual aircraft's exact configuration open.

abstractions.description: The playable target corridor and any cable sequence are authored around one reported contact rather than reconstructed from a surveyed historical obstacle layout.
abstractions.reason: Current evidence does not establish exact target coordinates, route, cable count, support geometry, height, spacing, or purpose, while gameplay requires visible physical collision geometry.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: Briefing, archive, replay, and debrief label the route and cable layout as reconstruction.

abstractions.description: Partial-wing damage uses a bounded controllability envelope and sensitivity-tested surrogate forces rather than claiming exact fracture or aerodynamic derivatives.
abstractions.reason: The account supplies damage scale and qualitative landing risk, but the relevant structure, controls, mass distribution, and damaged-flight data are not yet source-locked.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: The archive distinguishes reported wing loss from simulated handling and publishes the accepted reconstruction bounds.

abstractions.description: Radio lines perform documented communication functions in restrained period-informed language but do not claim to quote Armstrong, Carpenter, the Essex deck, or ground personnel.
abstractions.reason: No incident radio transcript is registered, and later dramatizations cannot be laundered into historical dialogue.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: Line-level provenance labels every unsourced utterance as procedural reconstruction and original performances do not imitate real voices.

abstractions.description: Ejection, parachute, landing, and ground recovery remain greybox-only placeholders until seat, procedure, location, wind, equipment, and independent recovery evidence close.
abstractions.reason: The broad survival sequence is supported, but current evidence cannot justify exact hardware behavior, acceleration, action order, trajectory, terrain, vehicle, dialogue, or interpersonal staging.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: No public historical release may present these details as exact; the archive names the unresolved fields.

abstractions.description: The 2034 sortie is a fictional transfer exercise that preserves the stabilization, observer-limited inspection, and survival-decision structure without repeating Armstrong's outcome.
abstractions.reason: Campaign governance requires historical knowledge to change the meaning of a later modern decision, while a real person's fixed biography must not become a branching sandbox.
abstractions.playerDisclosure: The mission selection, briefing, archive, and debrief identify the 2034 event and cast as fiction.

agencyRules: Armstrong is represented as a young naval aviator acting on observable aircraft and formation evidence, not through retrospective astronaut mythology or invented inner monologue.
Carpenter remains a professional actor with observer-limited knowledge, not an omniscient tutorial voice or a device for assigning Armstrong's decision to someone else.
Essex deck and ground-recovery personnel remain documented operational roles unless records support names, actions, and words.
The fixed historical outcome never converts player difficulty into blame for what happened to a real person.
No dialogue, performance direction, or visual motif uses Moon foreshadowing or imitates a real person's voice.
representation.civilianContext: Transportation and storage targets, the Wonsan region, friendly territory, and the ground-recovery area existed within a war affecting Korean civilians; target and terrain production must not reduce inhabited geography to an empty obstacle course.

Presenting the disputed cable-versus-antiaircraft-fire/pole account, target, cable field, exact damage, loadout, or radio script as settled fact.

Making ejection injury, parachute descent, or ground recovery into spectacle or comedy.
Implying endorsement by Armstrong's family, NASA, the U.S. Navy, NHHC, or an archive.
